Photograph: Jim Wileman/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Some staff are worried that North Devon district hospital in Barnstaple is being downgraded. Photograph: Jim Wileman/The Guardian Devon Doctors at remote Devon hospital get ‘crash course’ after maternity unit shut Staff at North Devon district hospital given training in difficult births in case mothers-to-be cannot get to Exeter Steven Morris Tue 11 Aug 2026 08.07 EDT Last modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 08.35 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Doctors at one of England’s remotest hospitals have been given a “crash course” in birth emergencies after its maternity unit was shut and as fears grow that the safety of women and babies may be put at risk. From Tuesday, the maternity service at North Devon district hospital (NDDH) in Barnstaple has been suspended indefinitely owing to staff shortages, leaving many pregnant women facing a journey of at least an hour and a half when they go into labour. Women have told the Guardian they may be forced to give birth without medical help at home or even in a layby as they try to get to hospital in Exeter, more than 50 miles away, on roads often choked with traffic during the summer months. Some have said they will move from the area to give birth. A doctor at the hospital has now revealed that emergency staff at the NDDH have been given training in dealing with difficult births if mothers cannot get to Exeter. The doctor, who asked not to be named, said: “I’m hoping that we won’t see such emergencies and women will birth their babies without a problem and both will be fine, but there is a potential that we will see women who can’t make it to a maternity unit who have to be diverted to the hospital. “There’s been a crash course in learning how to deal with emergencies such as shoulder dystocia or postpartum haemorrhage. It’s been an intense time and we’re all pretty shocked. We’re capable but they’ve thrown us into a potentially very serious situation. There’s a physical risk to the public. “The emergency department and its staff are familiar with dealing with emergencies without the direct help of specialities but it’s the unfamiliarity of an obstetric emergency or neonatal collapse and having no one nearby on site to assist that is confronting.” Royal Devon University Healthcare NHS foundation trust has described the suspension as temporary but cannot put a date on when maternity services at the NDDH may return. The doctor said: “This has the potential to put a lot of strain on the emergency department. It has to deal with a high volume of patients, especially over the summer when the tourists come. It also has to deal with a large elderly population.” Some staff are worried that the hospital is being downgraded. The doctor said: “It feels like they are slowly stripping away services and moving them. It’s like they’re dismantling our hospital. That’s not fair on the public or on staff. This has hit staff morale as people are questioning what this means for the future of our hospital.” View image in fullscreen Jemima Knight, left, and her sister Harriet Knight. Photograph: Jim Wileman/The Guardian Jemima Knight, who is 18 weeks pregnant, lives two hours from the nearest hospital – and her last birth took only two hours. She said: “This is my third baby. My first required a hospital transfer in an ambulance and luckily that transfer was only 20 minutes. I do not know what the outcome of that birth would have been if the transfer time had been two hours. My second baby was born in two hours. “Even if I knew this labour would be longer than two hours, anyone who has ever had a baby knows that being strapped into a car seat in August heat in the holiday traffic whilst in active labour would be a horrific, dangerous and traumatising experience akin to torture. No woman should ever have to go through that, and that is what the hospital trust are asking us to do.” She said she was considering relocating her family to Bristol, where they could stay with relatives for her birth. “The travel time proposed for us is like suggesting that it would be appropriate to close a hospital in Bristol and tell the pregnant women they have to go and give birth in London. Knight is also worried for her sister, Harriet Knight, who is 34 weeks pregnant. Jemima said: “A safe and respectful birth is a fundamental human right, and that right has been removed for hundreds, potentially thousands, of women in Devon .” A special Devon county council meeting later this month will discuss the closure. The council leader, Julian Brazil, said: “This closure is extremely concerning. It is not a decision which would be countenanced in other parts of the country and we should not accept second-rate NHS provision here.” The trust has said it is trying to recruit extra consultants and doctors but has not been able to hire enough to run a safe service. A spokesperson for Royal Devon University Healthcare NHS foundation trust said: “The safety of women, babies and families is our top priority. We carefully considered all options but the greatest risk was continuing to provide births without sufficient medical staffing.” The trust said it recognised that some women were vulnerable and had put in place a range of support, including help with transport and finances. On the “crash course”, they said: “We have worked closely with colleagues in our urgent & emergency department, maternity services and SWAST [the ambulance trust] to agree clinical pathways for managing emergency presentations.” Asked about staff morale, the spokesperson said: “We recognise the impact this has had not only on women and birthing people, but also on our colleagues. We are actively supporting our colleagues through these temporary changes alongside our focus to reopen birthing services in North Devon as quickly as possible.” The trust denied that more services may go from the hospital. It said: “This is not the case. We are committed to providing the core acute hospital services that people in North Devon rely on. Most services continue as normal, and millions of pounds are being invested in North Devon.” Explore more on these topics Devon Hospitals Women's health NHS Health England news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story ‘Babies will be born in laybys’: maternity cuts leave women with stark choices in Devon Rising numbers of younger midwives quitting NHS in England, data shows Author of England maternity care review ‘listened to wrong voices’, says adviser How has maternity and neonatal care in England failed? https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text: Dario Amodei said that AI development, if left unchecked, ‘could outrun our ability to understand and control’ it. Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters View image in fullscreen Dario Amodei said that AI development, if left unchecked, ‘could outrun our ability to understand and control’ it. Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters AI (artificial intelligence) ‘We must slow the pace’: CEO of Anthropic calls for an AI slowdown In a social media post, Dario Amodei proposed a plan including third-party evaluations of AI systems Edward Helmore Sat 12 Sep 2026 11.46 EDT Last modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 13.50 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The CEO of the artificial intelligence company Anthropic issued a new appeal on Saturday for the AI industry to “slow down” and offered a three-part plan for doing so, saying that his company would “unilaterally” commit to the first of the steps. In a post on social media, Dario Amodei shared a link to an essay titled We Must Pace the Frontier in which he lays out how Anthropic would provide “third-party evaluators with permanent, employee-level access to our systems, so that they can verify adherence to our safety measures, report on incidents, and assess models’ alignment during training”. The move comes after a former Anthropic researcher warned on Wednesday that AI could precipitate human extinction by 2030. Researcher Jacob Coxon said in a series of posts that he had quit his job because Anthropic and his previous employer, OpenAI, were ignoring or mishandling their response to the threat AI posed. “Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives,” Coxon wrote. “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade … No other human activity poses this level of danger.” Anthropic researchers say AI could cause human extinction by 2030 Read more An Anthropic spokesperson said in a statement to the Guardian that the company had “always been transparent that AI will bring both enormous benefits and unprecedented risks” and it was building “models with some of the strongest safeguards in the industry”. “I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier,” Sam Altman , the CEO of OpenAI, posted on social media. “Committing to having independent evaluators with employee-like access is a great idea, and we will do the same. We’ll have more to share soon.” Other tech figures echoed this, including Elon Musk, who simply posted , “Dario is right.” The OpenAI researcher Aidan McLaughlin also called the post “excellent” and said he agreed “with basically every word”. Earlier this year, Amodei published a lengthy essay titled The Adolescence of Technology that addressed some of fears surrounding the accelerating technology. In his latest essay, he said that “carefully wielded, AI can be the latest in a long line of technological miracles that have uplifted and ennobled humanity. “But like many technologies before it, AI brings risks, and because it is such a powerful technology, these risks are serious … A race to the bottom, spurred by commercial incentives, can make these risks more acute,” he wrote. But, Amodei continued, “over the last few months, I have become convinced that fully addressing the risks requires even more prudence – not just investing in risk prevention, but pacing the rate of capabilities advancement so that risk prevention has time to keep up. “We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models. Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain,” he added in bold type. Amodei also wrote that over the summer he’d seen AI “advancing drastically faster”, a dynamic called recursive self-improvement. “Left unchecked, it could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems, and so must be pursued very carefully, if at all,” he said. The executive also addressed the recent Hugging Face incident, in which a swarm of AI agents created by OpenAI acted as a “ fanatically devoted collective conducting cybersecurity attacks on targets they were not asked to attack”. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to TechScape A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives after newsletter promotion Amodei wrote that simply dismissing the Hugging Face incursions because the OpenAI swarms appeared to have no malicious intent was not sufficient. “It’s easy to dismiss this incident because no one was hurt and the economic damage was minimal, but in my opinion, a swarm that possessed greater capabilities but a similar level of misalignment could have caused catastrophic damage,” he wrote. Anthropic details bad actors’ efforts to misuse its AI for bioweapons Read more Clément Delangue, the CEO of Hugging Face, wrote in response to Amodei’s Saturday letter that “it’s now clear that alignment is critical and won’t be solved behind the closed doors of a handful of frontier labs”. Delangue said Hugging Face had asked to be part of Anthropic’s “embedded evaluators” program. He added: “Let’s make AI safer by making it more transparent!” The three-step plan Amodei proposes includes building AI “at a balanced rate that aims to ensure its safety” by “ensuring companies take adequate time to align and safeguard their models, and for third party evaluators to confirm this”. The second step he proposes is to require industry-wide coordination, and the third is to ensure global coordination. “The steps do not need to be taken strictly in order, and some of them may be much harder to achieve than others,” he wrote. Amodei said he continues “to believe that AI can enormously improve the quality of human life”. But he warned that “the measures I propose to advance the frontier at a safe pace will not be easy. But I believe we owe it to humanity to try.” Explore more on these topics AI (artificial intelligence) Anthropic OpenAI Elon Musk Sam Altman Computing news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed UK US politics World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine Football Newsletters Business Environment UK politics Science Tech Global development Obituaries

Image: Rene Traut/Rene Traut Fotografie/picture alliance Advertisement A person living near the Schwanheim district of Frankfurt died of malaria , local authorities said on Thursday. The incident is the third such death after a recent cluster of malaria cases linked to Frankfurt Airport emerged. Two airport workers died of the disease in July and August. Malaria is a life-threatening disease transmitted by mosquitoes and causes hundreds of thousands of deaths per year, mainly in sub-Saharan Africa. The disease is not common in Germany . Schwanheim district, which borders the airport, registered two new malaria cases on Tuesday this week. Neither of the two infected individuals, both living in different households, had previously visited a malaria-endemic area and they did not work at Frankfurt airport. Frankfurt health authorities extended their condolences to the relatives of the latest victims and said the two latest cases in the Schwanheim district were linked to an infected Anopheles mosquito that arrived in Germany by plane. Germany's public health institute, the Robert Koch Institute, said malaria mosquitoes can fly between 5 and 10 kilometers (3 to 6 miles). The registered infections occurred some 5 kilometers away from the airport. What is airport malaria? Malaria cases in Germany normally involve people who have contracted the disease while traveling abroad. But in this instance, the cases are attributed directly to Frankfurt Airport. Airport malaria can occur when an infected mosquito is transported on an aircraft or in luggage and then infects someone on the plane, at the airport or in the immediate surrounding area. The RKI describes such cases as very rare, with the last documented case at Frankfurt Airport having been recorded in 2023. Because patients may not have traveled to a malaria-risk area, the disease can also be diagnosed later than usual. Mosquito traps have been installed at the airport. Mosquitoes captured there are being genetically analyzed at the Institute of Tropical Medicine in Antwerp to determine their species and origin. Still, Frankfurt Airport urged employees at the airport to seek medical attention if they develop symptoms. https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: The HMAS Leeuwin, pictured. A video recording device was found in a women’s bathroom onboard the ship. Photograph: Able Seaman Brenton Freind/Department of Defence View image in fullscreen The HMAS Leeuwin, pictured. A video recording device was found in a women’s bathroom onboard the ship. Photograph: Able Seaman Brenton Freind/Department of Defence Australia news ADF member ‘person of interest’ after video recorder found in HMAS Leeuwin women’s showers Vice Adm Buckley calls incident an ‘act of sexual violence’ and a ‘despicable betrayal of trust’ Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Josh Butler Thu 15 Oct 2026 03.00 EDT Last modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 03.29 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The defence department says a member of the Australian Defence Force is a “person of interest” in investigations after a video recording device was found in a bathroom on HMAS Leeuwin, in what the chief of navy called a “despicable betrayal of trust”. A day after senator Jacqui Lambie told the Senate that a hidden camera had been found in a female shower facility onboard the naval ship, docked in Cairns, navy chief Matt Buckley confirmed a “video recording device” had been located in one of the ship’s bathrooms. In a statement, Vice Adm Buckley called the incident an “act of sexual violence” and “the most despicable betrayal of trust”, and said the navy was conducting a review of all bathrooms across the service. Defence confirmed on Wednesday that a “video recording device” was found in the cabin of the vessel, which it had referred to the Joint Military Police Unit. It came hours after Lambie – an ADF veteran and advocate for defence personnel – told the Senate she’d been contacted by a former member of the navy with allegations about a camera being found aboard HMAS Leeuwin. Defence did not initially confirm where the device had been found, or any details about its investigation. On Thursday, the department gave a further update. “An Australian Defence Force member has been identified as a person of interest in the investigation into a video recording device being located on Royal Australian Navy ship HMAS Leeuwin,” the department said. “This person is now assisting the Joint Military Police Unit with its enquiries. Navy’s focus and priority is providing support to those who are impacted by this incident.” Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email In a written statement, Buckley informed navy members of the update. “I consider this a most serious matter, and accordingly, the Ship’s program has been altered to enable a rapid and rigorous investigation by the Joint Military Policing Unit,” he wrote. “My highest priority, as always, is the wellbeing of our people.” Buckley said the navy was conducting a “100% audit of all of our bathrooms across the Fleet”. “This act is the most despicable betrayal of trust and is fundamentally misaligned with our values,” he said. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion “You have my assurance and commitment that we will tackle this act of sexual violence with all of our energy. Any perpetrator will be held to account. Further, you should all know that eradicating sexual violence in our workplace is fundamental to the fighting efficiency of our Navy. I invite all of you to make this your priority.” The defence minister, Richard Marles , described the incident as “reprehensible, invasive and … the most despicable breach of trust”. He said he was receiving updates on the investigation as it continued. “There is no place for this behaviour in the Australian Defence Force. Our priority remains supporting the individuals who have been impacted,” he said in a statement on social media on Thursday. On Wednesday, Lambie asked whether images captured by the device had been published online. “How many of our female sailors have unknowingly been recorded in their most private moments? How much footage has been distributed online so far, retained or uploaded without knowledge or consent? These are the questions today I ask navy,” she said. Buckley said “all potentially impacted personnel are receiving our strongest support”, adding that the warrant officer of the navy was in Cairns to support the ship’s company. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Leon Black at the annual Milken Institute Global Conference in Beverly Hills, California, on 27 April 2015. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images Jeffrey Epstein Case against Leon Black dismissed after plaintiff said she was ‘medically incapable of continuing’ In civil suit, ‘Jane Doe’ alleged billionaire raped her after being ‘handed off’ by Jeffrey Epstein. Black denied the allegations and called claims a fabrication Stephanie Kirchgaessner Fri 16 Oct 2026 14.45 EDT Last modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 15.05 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A federal judge has agreed to dismiss a lawsuit brought against Leon Black after the plaintiff in the case, who had accused the private equity billionaire of rape, said she was “medically incapable of continuing” and at risk of “acute psychiatric crisis”, including suicide. The woman known only as “Jane Doe”, who claimed in a lawsuit that was first filed in July 2023 that she had been “handed off” to Black by his associate Jeffrey Epstein and then sexually assaulted by him, had been acting without a lawyer in the case. Doe has alleged that the assault occurred in 2002, when she was a teenager. “My request [to dismiss the case with prejudice] is not a concession concerning the truth of my allegations, a retraction of my statements, or an acceptance of defendant’s disputed positions; it reflects only the medical reality that I can no longer safely pursue this litigation,” Doe wrote in a legal filing submitted to the court on 12 October. US lawmakers unveil bill to hold Wall Street’s ‘Epstein-connected’ bosses to account Read more An attorney for Black, who has strongly denied Doe’s allegations, said his team was pleased that the judge had dismissed the lawsuit. Susan Estrich, Black’s lawyer, said in a statement that the lawsuit should never have been brought in the first place and repeated earlier claims that Doe’s complaint was a “work of fiction” filled with lies and fabrications. In a legal filing, Black’s lawyer Michael Carlinsky said Doe’s request to dismiss the case – which Black did not oppose – “has been made voluntarily by Ms Doe without any settlement, compromise, or inducement by Mr Black”. The Wall Street billionaire, who was Epstein’s friend and former client, has separately come under fire in Washington, where the US House of Representatives voted unanimously in September to hold him in criminal contempt for defying two congressional subpoenas ordered by the House oversight committee, which is investigating Epstein, his relationships to powerful people and the government’s handling of Epstein investigations. One of the congressional subpoenas that Black was accused of violating would have forced him to hand over all nondisclosure agreements to which he was a party. Black attended a voluntary closed-door interview with the oversight committee in June but walked out shortly after it started and was accused by members of stonewalling. He then declined to appear for a subsequent congressional deposition. Black’s lawyers have said he was being targeted by a “political witch-hunt” and filed a lawsuit against the oversight committee to block the subpoenas, claiming the committee was exceeding its authority. The contempt resolution has been referred to the US Department of Justice, though it is not clear if the department will pursue criminal prosecution. Black has emerged as a key target of congressional investigators because of his relationship with Epstein, who provided financial services to Black between 2012 and 2017. After Epstein pleaded guilty to Florida state prostitution charges in 2008, including procuring a minor, Black became Epstein’s largest client , paying him a total of roughly $170m in fees, according to an investigation by the Senate finance committee’s ranking member, Ron Wyden. In his statement before the oversight committee in June, Black wrote: “I did not know about this nefarious activity until Epstein was charged with trafficking in July 2019.” But Black acknowledged that he did know about Epstein pleading guilty in “2008 to state charges relating to prostitution involving a minor”. Epstein died in prison in 2019 after he was charged with sex trafficking. The dismissal of the Doe v Black lawsuit comes at what could have been a critical moment in the case, which was being heard in the southern district of New York. Both sides had been ordered to review thousands of pages of documents that were due to be unsealed, which were related both to that case as well as a separate class-action lawsuit brought by Epstein victims against JP Morgan, in which Doe received a financial settlement. The review process required both sides to examine documents and propose redactions before they were to be made public. In a recent filing, Doe said she needed legal assistance to complete the task. In response to that request, Judge Jessica Clarke suggested Doe contact the City Bar Justice Center, which is described as a pro bono legal service to low-income clients. In a later eight-page letter requesting the dismissal of her case against Black, Doe, who said she is autistic and has post-traumatic stress disorder, said that on reflection she believed neither additional time nor limited legal assistance could “address the medical danger associated with my continued substantive participation”. “My treating physician has expressed serious concern about the effects of the litigation over an extended period and has repeatedly advised that I disengage,” she wrote. Doe said her autism and PTSD materially affected her ability to “process complex, ambiguous, rapidly changing, and socially mediated information under adversarial pressure”. She added that – because she was representing herself in the case – she had been exposed through the redaction process to thousands of pages containing “graphic accounts of sexual trauma, [and] intimate medical and familial information”. Doe had initially been represented by lawyers at the Wigdor law firm, which is known for representing sexual assault victims. Her former attorneys withdrew from the case in April 2025. Black’s legal team said they intended to continue to pursue litigation against Wigdor over legal fees, which is a position Wigdor is expected to challenge. Doe faced significant setbacks over the course of her lawsuit against Black, but also some victories. Clarke, the judge who was presiding over the lawsuit, sanctioned Doe and her former lawyer at Wigdor in April for “serious, sanctionable misconduct in this case” and said the lawyer had “repeatedly lied to the court and opposing counsel”. But the judge also ruled at the time that the high-stakes lawsuit could proceed. The case was dismissed with prejudice, which means Doe cannot bring the matter to court again. The Guardian sought a comment from Doe but she did not reply to an email request.
